chapters.html:
Introduction

Spoken conversational agents are rapidly expanding beyond brief voice commands into long-form, semi-structured enterprise workflows such as qualitative user research, clinical intake, oral assessment, and structured interviewing. Although end-to-end speech-to-speech duplex models have demonstrated compelling overlap generation in casual banter, production enterprise deployments remain overwhelmingly governed by modular (cascaded) voice-agent pipelines (Silero VAD → Turn Detector → ASR / Tool-Use LLM → TTS) where deterministic tool execution, prompt guardrails, hallucination control, and text-level compliance auditing are non-negotiable. Within modular pipelines, end-of-utterance (EOU) detection acts as a discrete commit gate: once triggered, the pipeline dispatches LLM generation and TTS playback, so premature turn-taking cuts off multi-clause interviewee reasoning during 300–600ms cognitive pauses while conservative silence timers render the agent sluggish [1][2].

Why Existing Benchmarks Misrank Interview Turn Detectors.

Despite rapid progress in open-source turn detectors [3][4][5][6] and public leaderboards [7][8][9][10], selecting an endpointing model for modular bilingual interviews from existing benchmarks introduces systematic evaluation blind spots:

  1. Retrospective floor-end vs. Causal response-ready: Public voice-agent leaderboards such as LiveKit eot-bench (https://livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench) [7] derive labels retrospectively from logs—marking only the final pause of an observed turn as EOT (floor-end) and all earlier pauses as HOLD. In multi-sentence responses, this convention penalizes natural mid-interview transition-relevance places [11] where an interviewee completes a coherent thought and only elaborates because the agent stays silent.

  2. Short Assistant Queries vs. Multi-Clause Interviews: Single-intent assistant turns rarely exhibit the 300–600ms clause-internal thinking pauses typical of spoken interviews, masking short-horizon memory bottlenecks in streaming audio-only models while understating the value of preceding interviewer context.

  3. System-Modular, Perception-Audio-Native Conditioning: Turn-taking literature frequently conflates modular voice-agent pipelines with legacy ASR-cascaded text endpointing (User Audio → Streaming ASR → Text LLM), which incurs streaming ASR latency and discards prosodic cues. In reality, a modular pipeline can ingest raw user waveform prosody directly without user ASR while conditioning on its own deterministic, zero-latency, zero-WER agent_text—information completely absent in zero-context benchmarks (EasyTurn-800 [5]) and noisy in spontaneous human-human recordings (TurnBench [8]).

To close this evaluation gap, our primary contribution in this report is the construction, human blind audit, and public gated release of Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, paired with a comprehensive cross-benchmark ranking analysis across open-source baselines and our proprietary Pikaia-Turn reference model family:

  • Public Gated Release of Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 (Section 3): We release 2,338 strictly causal bilingual decision points (978 Mandarin, 1,360 English) across 150 speaker-disjoint clusters and 1,700 sample-verified 300ms/600ms prefix pairs (5,459 WAV files). Partitioned into auto-gated development (dev, N=100), manual-gated research evaluation (test, N=1,100), and strictly private blind holdout (test_private, N=1,138) tiers with zero speaker or asset overlap, the benchmark achieves 90.11% definitive dual-human blind agreement (κ=0.8024) under a causal response-ready contract.

  • Multi-Tier Reference Evaluation with the Proprietary Pikaia-Turn Family (Section 4, Section 5): To establish strong cross-modal reference frontiers across cloud GPU and pure-CPU streaming budgets without leaking benchmark speakers, we evaluate three open-source zero-shot detectors (Smart Turn v3.2 [8M], Turn-1-Mini [5.3M], and Turn-1 [2.3B]) alongside three proprietary Pikaia-Turn models:1 Pikaia-Turn (2.3B; 0.9619 Tier 2 AUC, 63.66% full-benchmark R@1% FPR), standalone Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B; 0.9680 600ms AUC, 395.3ms full-cascade wait), and pure-CPU streaming Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M; +32.78pp Tier 2 R@5% over Turn-1-Mini).

  • Leaderboard Ranking Shifts and Dyadic Stress Testing (Section 6): We document concrete ranking reversals between livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench and Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 across both server and CPU tiers (Table 5, Table 6), show that fine-tuning open-source Smart Turn v3.2 under our response-ready interview paradigm climbs +2 to +5 positions on the public 13-system LiveKit eot-bench leaderboard (English #5→#3 at ≤2% and #9→#5–#6 at ≤10%; Mandarin #7→#2–#3 at ≤5%), and characterize spontaneous human-human dyadic boundaries on TurnBench Dev.

  • Controlled Data and Architecture Ablations Across Public and Interview Suites (Section 7): Varying supervision scale (0→2,025→3,195 clips) and unmodified vs. modified architectures across Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, LiveKit eot-bench (Table 8), and zero-context EasyTurn-800 (Table 9), we track 300ms/600ms accuracy and recall alongside ≤5% FPR recall and mean waiting latency, demonstrating zero catastrophic forgetting across both unmodified and modified models trained on our corpus.

  1. Throughout this report, Pikaia-Turn (2.3B) denotes our flagship dual-backbone server model, Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B) denotes our standalone single-backbone server model, and Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M) denotes our pure-CPU causal streaming model, clearly distinguished from the 5.3M open-source audio-only baseline Turn-1-Mini. While Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 is publicly released under gated research terms, Pikaia-Turn weights remain proprietary.↩︎

Related Work

Turn-Taking in Modular Voice Agents vs. Full-Duplex Human Dialogue.

Foundational conversation analysis established that human turn transitions minimize both gap and overlap by projecting transition-relevance places (TRPs) jointly from syntax, pragmatics, and prosody [11][1]. Classical modular dialogue pipelines relied on VAD paired with fixed silence timeouts or handcrafted task-state rules [2], which break down in open-ended interviews where within-turn cognitive pauses routinely exceed 500ms. Conversely, self-supervised Voice Activity Projection (VAP) models [3][12] and end-to-end full-duplex speech-to-speech models predict continuous multi-party frame activity directly from dual-channel audio. While well suited to overlapping human-human chitchat, enterprise voice agents predominantly retain a modular VAD → Turn Detector → ASR / LLM → TTS architecture for tool-use determinism and auditability, where turn-taking acts as a discrete commit gate and the agent’s preceding prompt is already known as clean text prior to user speech.

Spoken Turn-Taking Benchmarks and Public Leaderboards.

Contemporary benchmarks probe distinct operational regimes (Table 1). LiveKit eot-bench [7] maintains a widely referenced public leaderboard (https://livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench) comparing 13 commercial and open-source turn detectors on false cut-off rate versus mean waiting time in task-oriented human-agent turns, defining only the final pause of an observed turn as EOT (floor-end) and all earlier pauses as HOLD. EasyTurn-800 [5] evaluates single-turn Mandarin utterances without preceding dialogue context across real human recordings and CosyVoice-2 synthetic TTS, introducing diagnostic subsets for backchannels (Backchannel-100) and explicit hold commands (Wait-100). TurnBench [8] provides studio-recorded two-speaker English human-human conversations where interlocutors frequently take the floor within <300ms or in overlap. In full-duplex evaluation, TACT [9] separates physical timing from intent-conditioned response windows using hindsight context, while ECHO [10] pairs identical interruption utterances with rewritten Mandarin contexts on synthetic audio. Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 complements these suites by targeting real non-studio bilingual human-agent interviews under strict causal truncation and blind-audited response-ready labels, exposing substantial model ranking shifts relative to floor-end leaderboards.

Audio-Native Semantic and Cross-Modal End-of-Turn Detectors.

Recent turn detectors replace ASR-based text endpointing with direct neural encoding of user waveforms. Open-source Smart Turn v3 [4] adapts an 8M Whisper acoustic encoder [13] over 8s causal windows for audio-only EOU classification. EasyTurn [5] integrates acoustic and linguistic representations in a speech-LLM framework, while p99lab/turn-1 [6] combines Qwen3-ASR [14] backbones (1.7B+0.6B=2.3B) alongside Turn-1-Mini (5.3M), a compact pure-CPU causal streaming audio-only transformer. Alongside evaluating these open-source checkpoints and quantifying how Smart Turn v3.2 shifts rank on LiveKit eot-bench when fine-tuned under our response-ready paradigm, we report reference results from our proprietary Pikaia-Turn family (Section 4) across 2.3B dual-backbone server, 0.6B standalone server, and 6.7M pure-CPU causal streaming tiers.

The Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 Dataset

Task Formulation: Causal response-ready vs. Retrospective floor-end

In semi-structured research interviews, an interviewee often answers a multi-part question in stages: delivering a complete, coherent thought, pausing for 300–600ms, and then optionally elaborating if the interviewer remains silent. Under a retrospective floor-end convention (as used in task-dialogue logs such as LiveKit eot-bench [7]), any pause followed by further speech from the same speaker is labeled HOLD, even when taking the floor at that pause would have been completely natural. Conversely, an observed turn end in production logs can reflect premature agent barge-in rather than genuine speaker completion.

To align evaluation with discrete response commitment in modular voice agents without leaking future information, we adopt a strictly causal response-ready specification:

Given the preceding interviewer prompt q and the interviewee’s causal audio waveform x≤tc truncated at pause cutoff tc, is it pragmatically, syntactically, and prosodically natural for the interviewer to begin responding at tc without cutting off an unfinished thought?

Crucially, subsequent same-speaker continuation after tc does not retroactively invalidate a valid response-ready transition point, nor does surface syntactic completeness imply EOT when prosodic continuation cues (e.g., non-final pitch contour, audible inhalation, lexical hesitations, or explicit “one moment” requests) project an ongoing turn. Table 1 situates Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 alongside the three external benchmarks evaluated in Section 6, Section 7—LiveKit eot-bench [7] (modular human-agent task dialogue), EasyTurn-800 [5] (zero-context single-turn Mandarin), and TurnBench Dev [8] (spontaneous two-speaker human-human conversation).

Curation, Privacy Remediation, and Three-Tier Partitioning

Candidate decision points were extracted from real consented Mandarin Chinese (zh) and English (en) spoken research interviews conducted over consumer microphones and telephony/WebRTC channels. Every decision point provides a primary causal observation at 300ms of trailing pause (16kHz mono PCM16 WAV) and, whenever uninterrupted post-cutoff recording persisted to 600ms, a sample-exact extended observation.

Prior to freezing v1.0.0, we executed a comprehensive compliance, privacy, and signal-integrity remediation audit:

  1. Consent and Age-Verification Filtering: Three speaker clusters (68 items) with unverified age or external consent scope were permanently removed at the cluster level, and one additional cluster (40 items) where a participant self-described as a high-school student without verified adult documentation was quarantined and excluded.

  2. Internal-Team and Sensitive-Content Isolation: Seventeen clips containing sensitive operational disclosures were removed, and all remaining 88 internal-team test clips were isolated exclusively into the private Tier 3 holdout so that public distributions contain zero internal personnel recordings.

  3. Sample-Exact 300ms/600ms Prefix Verification: In earlier release candidates, 157 nominal 600ms pairs were discovered to be byte-identical to their 300ms clips due to recording boundary truncation. After removing 26 with excluded clusters, we revoked the invalid 600ms pairing on the remaining 131 items (retaining their valid 300ms clips). Every one of the 1,700 retained pairs in v1.0.0 is verified to satisfy exact PCM prefix equality x1:L(600)≡x1:L(300) and exact length delta L600−L300=4,800 samples (300.0ms at 16kHz).

As summarized in Table 2, Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 comprises 2,338 decision points (978 Mandarin across 40 speaker clusters; 1,360 English across 115 speaker clusters) and 5,459 verified WAV files (2,338 user 300ms clips, 1,700 user 600ms clips, and 1,421 preceding interviewer audio prompts). To support reproducible calibration while preventing benchmark overfitting and protecting participant privacy, we partition the 150 speaker clusters into three strictly speaker-disjoint and WAV-disjoint tiers:

  • Tier 1 (dev, N=100, 11 clusters): Balanced 50 ZH / 50 EN development and threshold-calibration split, hosted under automatic gated terms at pikaia-ai/interview-eou-benchmark.

  • Tier 2 (test, N=1,100, 65 clusters): Primary external research evaluation split (500 ZH / 600 EN; 788 verified 600ms pairs), hosted under manually reviewed non-commercial academic access at pikaia-ai/interview-eou-benchmark-research.

  • Tier 3 (test_private, N=1,138, 74 clusters): Strictly private blind holdout (428 ZH / 710 EN; 837 verified 600ms pairs) used to verify that findings on Tier 2 generalize without public test-set exposure.

Label Provenance and Dual-Human Blind Listening Audit

Each item carries an explicit provenance tier recording how its reference label was established: 1,382 historical_postcutoff items inherited from validated multi-stage interview curation, 471 causal_reviewed items verified under causal cutoff review, 477 causal_new Mandarin expansion items annotated strictly from pre-cutoff context and audio, and 8 human_adjudicated items resolved during blind human audit. In Section 5, we report model performance both overall and stratified across causal versus historical provenance subsets to verify that model rankings are not artifacts of historical label provenance.

To quantify human reliability on the causal response-ready task, two independent bilingual human reviewers conducted a two-stage blind listening audit on a stratified sample of 100 items spanning 78 distinct speaker clusters, listening exclusively to the preceding interviewer question and causal 300ms-cutoff user audio without access to reference labels, model predictions, or post-cutoff continuation. Among the 91 items where both blind listeners rendered definitive binary judgments (9 flagged uncertain), raw inter-annotator agreement reached 90.11% (82/91; Mandarin 93.75%, English 86.05%), with Horvitz–Thompson [15] sampling-weighted agreement of 89.05% and Cohen’s κ=0.8024 [16] (95% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.6706,0.9115]). Comparing the independent external reviewer against pre-audit reference labels yielded 89.01% raw agreement (81/91; Mandarin 87.50%, English 90.70%), Horvitz–Thompson weighted agreement of 92.31%, and κ=0.7803 (95% CI [0.6383,0.9096]). Within the 94 audited items retained after compliance filtering, definitive dual-human agreement is 90.59% (77/85).

Causal Input Tracks and Disjoint Training Corpus

The benchmark defines three strictly causal evaluation tracks: (i) audio_only, supplying only the interviewee’s causal waveform up to tc; (ii) audio_plus_agent_text, adding the text of the interviewer’s preceding prompt (causally truncated if interrupted before completion)—the native zero-latency operating mode of modular voice agents, where the agent’s own LLM/TTS text is deterministically known without ASR; and (iii) audio_plus_agent_audio, supplying preceding interviewer audio alongside causal user audio.

For reference model adaptation, we curated a strictly speaker-disjoint private bilingual interview training corpus under the same response-ready contract. All primary Pikaia-Turn checkpoints in this report are trained exclusively on a zero-contamination corpus of 3,195 causal clips (167 human-verified gold clips, 1,858 bilingual causal interview clips, and 1,170 expanded Mandarin interview clips; in Section 7, we systematically compare against the 2,025-clip pre-expansion subset across unmodified and modified architectures), paired with an independent internal bilingual validation/test split (Internal-Val, N=450; Internal-Test, N=431). We verified zero speaker-cluster overlap and zero PCM overlap between all training manifests and all three tiers of Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, Internal-Val/Test, LiveKit eot-bench, EasyTurn-800, and TurnBench Dev.

Overview of the Pikaia-Turn Model Family

In a modular voice-agent pipeline (Silero VAD → Turn Detector → ASR / Tool-Use LLM → TTS), whether a pause invites a discrete turn commit depends jointly on raw acoustic-prosodic completion cues at the user’s pause boundary and pragmatic expectations established by the agent’s deterministic agent_text prompt (for example, a closed confirmation question versus an open “walk me through three challenges” prompt). Because production deployments span cloud GPU clusters and CPU-only or edge workers, we develop the proprietary Pikaia-Turn model family across three compute tiers—Pikaia-Turn (2.3B), Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B), and Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M)—and benchmark them directly against three representative open-source zero-shot detectors (Smart Turn v3.2 [4], 5.3M Turn-1-Mini, and 2.3B Turn-1 [6]).

Cross-Modal Interface and Zero-Contamination Adaptation

All three Pikaia-Turn models share a unified causal runtime contract tailored to modular voice agents:

  • Asymmetric Audio-Native Inputs: At each candidate pause cutoff tc (300ms or 600ms), the detector ingests the user’s raw causal waveform x≤tc directly without waiting for streaming user ASR, conditioned on the preceding agent_text and language indicator (zh / en) to output a calibrated response-ready probability pEOT∈[0,1]. Unlike standard ASR text normalizers that strip punctuation, agent_text preprocessing preserves terminal and clause punctuation (such as question marks and enumerative prompts) that signal expected answer structure.

  • Single-Checkpoint Zero-Context Fallback: During training on our speaker-disjoint 3,195-clip causal interview corpus (Section 3), agent_text is stochastically dropped out (agent_text="") so that a single frozen checkpoint supports both context-conditioned modular pipelines (audio_plus_agent_text) and zero-context (audio_only) evaluations without separate weights or runtime reconfiguration.

Compute Tiers Across Server GPU and Pure-CPU Streaming

The three proprietary models cover complementary latency, memory, and hardware budgets:

  1. Pikaia-Turn (2.3B, Flagship Server Cross-Modal Detector): Pikaia-Turn operates at the 2.3B dual-backbone speech-LLM scale (1.7B+0.6B Qwen3-ASR lineage [14][6]) over causal user audio windows and preceding agent_text. Whereas zero-shot Turn-1 keeps its primary backbone frozen and relies on static boundary pooling—which can be diluted by trailing pause frames during 300–600ms silences—Pikaia-Turn jointly adapts cross-modal representations, speech-boundary prosodic pooling, and context-aware branch fusion for long-form bilingual interviews. It serves as our highest-accuracy cloud detector under ultra-strict (≤1%–5%) false-interruption budgets.

  2. Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B, Standalone Single-Backbone Server Detector): To eliminate dual-backbone inference overhead in high-concurrency GPU deployments, Pikaia-Turn-Mini operates as a standalone single-backbone cross-modal speech-LLM detector (0.6B parameters, roughly one-quarter of the 2.3B footprint [14]). By coupling multi-scale acoustic prosody representations with prompt-conditioned cross-modal readout, Pikaia-Turn-Mini matches the 3.8× larger zero-shot Turn-1 ensemble at 300ms while delivering the strongest discrimination across all models at extended 600ms pauses.

  3. Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M, Pure-CPU Causal Streaming Detector): For CPU-only servers and edge voice agents requiring frame-synchronous 160ms streaming without GPU acceleration, audio-only streaming baselines such as Turn-1-Mini (5.3M) [6] lack awareness of preceding agent_text and rapidly lose earlier clause context across >500ms pauses. Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M) pairs a causal streaming acoustic encoder with a lightweight turn-start prompt encoder (cached once before user speech begins, incurring zero per-chunk text overhead during audio streaming) and 𝒪(1) running utterance state, bringing cross-modal pragmatic conditioning to pure-CPU streaming while suppressing mid-utterance false triggers.

Benchmarking on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0

Evaluation Protocol, Latency–Cutoff Cascade, and Statistical Inference

Because premature agent barge-in disrupts interviewee reasoning in a modular voice pipeline, overall accuracy at an arbitrary τ=0.5 threshold is an unreliable proxy for deployment quality. Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 standardizes evaluation along three complementary axes: (i) Threshold-free and low-FPR discrimination, reporting ROC-AUC alongside empirical recall at strict HOLD false-positive budgets (≤1%, ≤3%, and ≤5% FPR, computed via exact count budgets ⌊αNHOLD⌋ with tie handling); (ii) Two-stage latency-versus-false-cutoff Pareto frontiers, adopting LiveKit eot-bench’s [7] operational visualization over paired 300ms/600ms items (N=1,700 on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0; N=842 on causal LiveKit eot-bench): a turn commits at 300ms if p300≥τ300, otherwise re-evaluates at 600ms if p600≥τ600, and falls back to a 1,000ms silence timeout otherwise, tracing the Pareto-optimal lower-left envelope of mean waiting latency on true EOTs versus cumulative false cut-off rate on true HOLDs; and (iii) Out-of-sample frozen-threshold transfer, locking language-specific thresholds (τzh,τen) on Tier 1 dev (N=100) or Internal-Val (N=450) and evaluating without adjustment on unseen Tier 2 test (N=1,100) and Tier 3 test_private (N=1,138). To account for within-speaker correlation across multiple turns from the same interviewee, all confidence intervals and two-sided p-values use paired cluster-stratified bootstrap (B=2,000 resamples over group_id speaker clusters stratified by language).

Main Discrimination and Waiting-Latency Frontiers Across Compute Tiers

Table 3 reports primary results across Tier 2 test, Tier 3 test_private, and the full 2,338-item benchmark. Figure 1 visualizes full-benchmark Mandarin and English ROC curves zoomed into the operational FPR∈[0,0.20] region, while Figure 2(a) plots the paired two-stage waiting-latency versus false-cutoff Pareto frontier (N=1,700).

Audio-Only Rank Inversion and Open-Source Adaptation Gains (5.3M–8M).

Evaluating open-source audio-only baselines on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 immediately exposes a sharp contrast with short-query assistant benchmarks (Section 6): whereas 5.3M streaming Turn-1-Mini substantially outperforms 8M Smart Turn v3.2 on LiveKit eot-bench, on multi-clause interviews Turn-1-Mini drops to last place (0.8240 full-benchmark AUC; 20.26% Tier 2 R@5%; 849.3ms Wait@5%) behind Smart Turn v3.2 (0.8444 AUC; 40.23% Tier 2 R@5%; 735.2ms Wait@5%), because Turn-1-Mini’s short local readout loses prior clause context across >300ms pauses. Adapting open-source Smart Turn v3.2 under our causal response-ready interview paradigm (3-seed mean) lifts full-benchmark AUC by +0.0484 to 0.8928 (p<0.0001), boosts Tier 2 R@5% by +23.56pp (40.23%→63.79%), and cuts paired two-stage Wait@5% by 104.4ms (735.2ms→630.8ms). Among pure-CPU streaming models, conditioning on deterministic agent_text and 𝒪(1) utterance state in proprietary Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M) raises full-benchmark AUC to 0.8737 (ΔAUC=+0.0498 over Turn-1-Mini, p<0.0001), boosts Tier 2 R@5% by +35.77pp (20.26%→56.03%), and cuts two-stage cascade waiting latency at ≤5% cut-off by 192.3ms (849.3ms→657.0ms; 605.3ms on Tier 2; Figure 2a).

Server Cross-Modal Speech-LLM Reference Frontiers (0.6B and 2.3B).

Zero-shot Turn-1 (2.3B) establishes a strong cross-modal baseline (0.9597 Tier 2 AUC; 0.9550 Full), yet its recall drops sharply under ultra-strict interruption budgets (40.78% full-benchmark recall at ≤1% FPR). Proprietary Pikaia-Turn (2.3B) achieves statistically significant gains across every split: 0.9658 AUC on Tier 2 (0.9839 ZH, 0.9447 EN; 84.48% R@5%), 0.9626 on blind Tier 3, and 0.9617 on the full benchmark (ΔAUC=+0.0067 over zero-shot Turn-1, 95% CI [+0.0035,+0.0104], p<0.0001), while surging full-benchmark 300ms recall at ≤1% FPR by +22.88pp (40.78%→63.66%) and reaching 377.2ms Wait@5% on Tier 2. Equally notable for GPU cost-efficiency, standalone Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B) matches 3.8× larger zero-shot Turn-1 at 300ms (0.9572 vs. 0.9550 on Full, p=0.380; 0.9611 vs. 0.9553 on blind Tier 3) and leads all models at the paired 600ms cutoff (0.9711 AUC and 90.79% R@5% on Tier 2; 0.9680 AUC and 86.17% R@5% on Full, ΔAUC=+0.0112 over Turn-1, p=0.002), achieving the lowest overall full-cascade waiting latency at ≤5% cut-off (395.3ms vs. 406.8ms for Pikaia-Turn and 411.4ms for zero-shot Turn-1; Figure 2a).

Out-of-Sample Frozen-Threshold Calibration Transfer

Real modular deployments must freeze scalar thresholds (τzh,τen) ahead of time rather than selecting hindsight-optimal ROC points. Table 4 evaluates strict out-of-sample threshold transfer from Tier 1 dev (N=100; 17 ZH / 18 EN HOLDs) to Tier 2 test and Tier 3 test_private, alongside transfer from Internal-Val (N=450). Under strict zero-FP calibration (FPdev=0), Pikaia-Turn recovers 68.78% of valid turn ends at 1.54% realized FPR on Tier 2 (63.11% at 1.48% FPR on blind Tier 3)—improving recall by +21.10pp over zero-shot Turn-1 (47.68% at 2.06% FPR) with fewer false interruptions. Under FPdev≤1 (≈5.7% nominal budget), all three Pikaia-Turn models transfer stably across Tier 2 and Tier 3 (78.76%/77.19% recall at 5.14%/4.19% FPR for Pikaia-Turn-Mini; 53.59%/53.14% at 4.37%/5.91% FPR for Pikaia-Turn-Nano), whereas uncalibrated zero-shot Smart Turn v3.2 jumps from 1.54% to 10.54% FPR due to upper-tail score clustering.

Provenance Stratification and Blind Human-Gold Consistency

As shown in Table 5 and Figure 3(a), stratifying Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 by label provenance confirms that model gains hold on purely causal and human-audited subsets rather than historical curation artifacts: while Pikaia-Turn (0.9795) and zero-shot Turn-1 (0.9789) are near ceiling on Historical Post-Cutoff (N=1,382), on Strictly Causal (N=956) Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.9478, +0.0245 over Turn-1) and Pikaia-Turn (0.9427, +0.0194) widen their lead, and on Dual-Human Blind Gold (N=77) Pikaia-Turn-Mini, Pikaia-Turn, and Pikaia-Turn-Nano reach 0.9771, 0.9696, and 0.9163 AUC (vs. 0.9597 for Turn-1 and 0.8367 for Turn-1-Mini). On independent Internal-Test (N=431), Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.8783 AUC, 39.80% R@5%) and Pikaia-Turn (0.8750 AUC, 39.12% R@5%) likewise beat zero-shot Turn-1 (0.8463 AUC, 24.49% R@5%) by >14.6pp; we examine full controlled Data × Architecture ablations across Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, LiveKit eot-bench, and EasyTurn-800 in Section 7.

Leaderboard Ranking Shifts and Dyadic External Evaluation

A central thesis of Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 is that turn-taking model rankings depend strongly on whether a benchmark evaluates causal response-ready vs. retrospective floor-end, multi-clause interviews vs. brief assistant commands, and modular human-agent pipelines vs. spontaneous human-human chitchat. In this section, we examine cross-benchmark ranking reversals on LiveKit eot-bench [7] (Section 6)—including slot-substitution rank tracking on the public 13-system livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench leaderboard—and stress-test out-of-domain spontaneous two-speaker chitchat on English TurnBench Dev [8] (Section 6), before turning to controlled Data × Architecture and zero-context EasyTurn-800 [5] ablations in Section 7.

Ranking Shifts Between LiveKit eot-bench and Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark

Table 5, Table 6 reveal three distinct ranking shifts that motivate Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 alongside public assistant leaderboards:

1. Objective-Driven Ranking Reversal on Paired Bilingual LiveKit eot-bench (Table 5, Figure 3b, Figure 2b).

Under original log-derived floor-end labels on bilingual LiveKit eot-bench (N=1,058 pairs: 455 ZH, 603 EN), zero-shot Turn-1 ranks #1 (583.2ms Wait@5%, 58.10% R@5%) ahead of Pikaia-Turn-Mini (#2, 631.1ms) and Pikaia-Turn (#3, 666.8ms, 46.65% R@5%). To test whether this reflects representation loss or label mismatch, we conducted a blind multi-annotator causal response-ready audit of the same 1,058 turns (N=842 unambiguous causal pairs) while keeping every model’s raw probability scores strictly unchanged. Re-scoring identical predictions flips the server ranking: Pikaia-Turn surges from #3 → #1 (+38.47pp R@5% to 85.12%; 394.4ms Wait@5%, saving 81.7ms over Turn-1), Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B) holds #2 (473.8ms Wait@5%, 73.53% R@5%) ahead of 3.8× larger zero-shot Turn-1 (#1 → #3, 476.1ms), and on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 (N=1,700 pairs) Pikaia-Turn-Mini rises to #1 overall cascade latency (395.3ms). Auditing discordant LiveKit items confirms why: users often complete a self-contained request, pause for 300–600ms, and append a polite clarifier only because the agent stays silent—a valid response-ready transition point that retrospective floor-end penalizes as a false cut-off.

2. Audio-Only Rank Inversion Between Public eot-bench and Long-Form Interviews (Table 5, Table 6).

On the official continuous LiveKit eot-bench English scorer (9ee21b5, 400 EOT / 705 HOLD, 11,191 causal queries), zero-shot 5.3M Turn-1-Mini achieves 1,349.8ms (≤2%), 848.8ms (≤5%), and 581.0ms (≤10%) mean wait (0.9017 AUC200), equivalent to #3#5 on the public 13-system leaderboard and >200ms faster at ≤5% than open-source Smart Turn v3.2 (1,051ms published #7; 1,045.3ms local #6; 0.8446 AUC200). On Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, however, their relative ranking completely inverts: Smart Turn v3.2 rises from #6 → #5 (735.2ms Wait@5%; 39.94% Tier 2 R@5%) while Turn-1-Mini drops to #6 (849.3ms Wait@5%; 20.53% Tier 2 R@5%), showing that short assistant benchmarks mask local-window memory forgetting in multi-clause spoken interviews.

3. Vaulting Open-Source Smart Turn v3.2 Up the Public LiveKit eot-bench Leaderboard (Table 6).

To test whether our causal response-ready interview supervision benefits third-party open-source architectures even on external leaderboards, we fine-tuned unmodified Smart Turn v3.2 (8M, 3 seeds {7,17,29}) on our bilingual interview data and evaluated it with the pinned official livekit/eot-bench harness across all 14 languages (5,454 turns, 125,703 decision points), substituting its mean waiting time into the Smart Turn v3.2 slot while keeping all 12 peer systems from livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench fixed.1 Across both languages, causal interview adaptation yields striking upward rank mobility:

  • English (13 Systems): Curated response-ready adaptation (2,900 clips) cuts mean wait at ≤2% cut-off from 1,762.8ms to 1,545.7ms (climbing #5 → #3, surpassing Gradium and ultraVAD, seeds {3,3,4}), trims ≤5% wait by 111.3ms to 933.9ms (#6, vs. #7 published), and cuts ≤10% wait by 66.5ms (95% paired cluster-bootstrap CI [+10.4,+161.9]ms) to 656.8ms (climbing #9 → #6), while lifting AUC200 from 0.8446→0.8901. Expanded bilingual adaptation (4,070 clips) pushes English ≤10% wait down to 641.3ms, climbing +4 spots from #9 → #5 ahead of Gradium, ultraVAD, LiveKit v1-mini, and AssemblyAI.

  • Mandarin (9 Systems) and 14-Language Transfer: Curated response-ready adaptation cuts Mandarin ≤5% wait to 861.9ms (climbing to #2/9 across all three seeds {2,2,2}, overtaking Soniox [886ms], LiveKit v1-mini [919ms], ultraVAD [926ms], and OpenAI GPT Realtime 2 [941ms]; +5 spots vs. published #7 and +1 vs. local #3) and ≤10% wait to 611.9ms (597.8ms on expanded strict FT, #3/9), while boosting Mandarin AUC200 from 0.7454→0.8324 and 14-language AUC200 from 0.7834→0.8357 (≤5% wait 929.3→898.3ms).

Out-of-Domain Stress Test: Spontaneous Human-Human Dyadic Speech on TurnBench Dev

Finally, Table 7 stress-tests our frozen checkpoints out-of-domain on spontaneous two-speaker human conversation (TurnBench Dev [8]: 38 studio English dyads; 1,904 EOT / 1,063 HOLD, official turnbench.score 38a6f874):

  • Why partner_asr Adds Zero Gain in Casual Chitchat: Conditioning on causal Whisper-base.en transcriptions of the partner’s preceding turn (partner_asr) yields no gain over user audio alone (86.08% vs. 86.19% single-channel and 91.28% vs. 91.28% duplex 5-fold OOF on Pikaia-Turn-Mini; 89.65% vs. 89.81% duplex OOF on Pikaia-Turn-Nano), confirming that agent_text conditioning specifically exploits structured, zero-WER modular agent prompts rather than unstructured human banter.

  • Preserved Acoustic Capacity Under Causal Duplex VAD Control: Under single-channel Legacy-1024ms gating (91.60% physical ceiling), frozen Pikaia-Turn-Mini reaches 86.19% Dev recall (84.51% OOF), beating zero-shot Turn-1 (85.14%), Turn-1-Mini (82.93%), and Smart Turn v3.2 (80.09% Dev; 75.2% published), while Pikaia-Turn-Nano’s slight 1.68pp conservatism (81.25%; 83.40% on an audio-only interview checkpoint) reflects its response-ready hold calibration. Pairing the exact same frozen weights with a lightweight causal (≤t) duplex partner-VAD state machine lifts Pikaia-Turn-Mini to 91.70% Dev / 91.28% OOF recall (617.5ms p50; 84.72% at 4.42% FPR) and Pikaia-Turn-Nano to 90.60% Dev / 89.81% OOF recall (597.0ms p50; 84.09% at 4.42% FPR).

Controlled Data and Architecture Ablations

To disentangle how domain supervision scale and cross-modal architectural design shape turn-taking behavior across both target interview deployments and external public benchmarks, we conduct a controlled Data × Architecture ablation across all four model families. Specifically, we vary training data across zero-shot checkpoints, the curated causal interview subset (2,025 clips), and the expanded bilingual interview corpus (3,195 clips; 3,891 clips for 3-seed open-source Smart Turn v3.2), while directly comparing unmodified open-source architectures against modified Pikaia-Turn architectures.

Capability Evolution Across Pikaia Benchmark v1.0.0 and Public LiveKit eot-bench

Table 8 reports single-cutoff τ=0.50 accuracy and recall (300ms and 600ms), strict low-interruption recall at ≤5% HOLD FPR (300ms and 600ms R@5%), and paired two-stage (300→600→1,000ms) cumulative recall and mean waiting latency at ≤5% false cut-off rate (Casc. R@5% and Wait@5%) across Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 and public LiveKit eot-bench (both causal response-ready and retrospective floor-end):

  1. 2.3B Dual-Backbone Family (Why Unmodified Fine-Tuning Regresses at Scale While Pikaia-Turn Eliminates Forgetting): Zero-shot Turn-1 suffers from severe threshold conservatism on multi-clause interviews (56.2%/32.4% accuracy/recall at 300ms and 54.1%/39.8% at 600ms under τ=0.50), yielding 411.4ms cascade Wait@5% on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 and 476.1ms on causal LiveKit eot-bench. Fine-tuning the unmodified Turn-1 readout on 2,025 curated clips aligns τ=0.50 operating points (86.6%/82.5% at 300ms; 87.2%/84.5% at 600ms) and improves cascade R@5% / Wait@5% on both Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 (84.4%/411.4ms→86.2%/398.4ms) and public LiveKit (77.1%/476.1ms→83.5%/425.5ms). However, scaling unmodified Turn-1 to 3,195 expanded interview clips triggers sharp external domain-shift regression: public LiveKit 600ms R@5% plunges by −23.1pp (83.8%→60.7%), external cascade Wait@5% degrades to 494.3ms (+18.2ms slower than zero-shot), and retrospective floor-end AUC drops −0.0422 (0.9109→0.8687). Jointly adapting cross-modal boundary pooling and context fusion in Pikaia-Turn eliminates this trade-off: at 2,025 clips Pikaia-Turn reaches 88.7% cascade R@5% and 387.8ms Wait@5% on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, while at 3,195 clips it simultaneously achieves 88.6%/86.3% (300ms) and 91.8%/91.5% (600ms) τ=0.50 accuracy/recall on Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, surges public LiveKit causal R@5% to 85.1% (300ms) and 87.5% (cascade) at 394.4ms Wait@5% (−81.7ms vs. zero-shot; −99.9ms vs. unmodified expanded FT), and preserves mismatched floor-end AUC (0.9038 vs. 0.9109).

Zero-Context Transfer and Anti-Forgetting on Public EasyTurn-800

To verify whether training on context-rich interviews degrades standalone acoustic turn detection when preceding agent prompts are unavailable, Table 9 and Figure 4 migrate our controlled Data × Architecture evaluation to public Mandarin EasyTurn-800 [5] (300 Real-300 human recordings, 300 Synthetic-300 CosyVoice-2 TTS utterances, 100 Backchannel-100, and 100 Wait-100), where agent_text="" across all 800 clips:

  1. Unmodified Architectures Trained on Our Corpus Improve Zero-Context Performance Without Catastrophic Forgetting: Even without modifying model architecture, fine-tuning open-source Turn-1 (2.3B) on our 2,025-clip curated interview dataset improves external zero-context EasyTurn-800 across nearly every metric: All-600 AUC rises from 0.9435→0.9472, Real-300 human AUC rises from 0.9571→0.9619, All-600 R@1% FPR jumps by +14.0pp (29.7%→43.7%), default @0.50 accuracy surges by +26.6pp (56.7%→83.3%), frozen out-of-sample ZH-ValCal recall rises by +19.6pp (39.7%→59.3% at 2.3% FPR), and matched-5% Backchannel-100 and Wait-100 hold accuracies climb from 82.0%→89.0% and 28.0%→38.0% while preserving 74.0% Real-300 completion recall. Similarly, fine-tuning unmodified Turn-1-Mini (5.3M) on our 2,025-clip corpus boosts All-600 AUC by +4.77pp (0.6626→0.7103) and Real-300 AUC by +5.82pp (0.6502→0.7084).

  2. Modified Pikaia-Turn Models Further Advance Calibration, Low-FPR Recall, and Backchannel Suppression: At the 2,025-clip curated scale, modified Pikaia-Turn achieves the highest All-600 AUC (0.9493), Synthetic-300 AUC (0.9353), frozen ZH-ValCal recall (64.3% at 4.7% FPR, +24.6pp over zero-shot Turn-1), and 2.3B Wait-100 hold (42.0%), while modified Pikaia-Turn-Nano (6.7M) lifts All-600 AUC by +10.36pp (0.6626→0.7662) and All-600 R@5% by +22.3pp (8.0%→30.3%, achieving 30.3% recall at 5.0% FPR under ZH-ValCal vs. 38.0% FPR on zero-shot Turn-1-Mini). At the 3,195-clip expanded scale, Pikaia-Turn reaches the highest default @0.50 accuracy (86.3%, +29.6pp), 61.7% ZH-ValCal recall at 4.7% FPR (+22.0pp), 39.0% R@1% FPR (+9.3pp), and preserved Real-300 human AUC (0.9573 vs. 0.9571), while standalone Pikaia-Turn-Mini (0.6B) improves across data scales (0.9030→0.9060 All-600 AUC) and cuts Backchannel-100 false triggers at matched 5% FPR from 18.0% down to 3.0% (97.0% hold accuracy; Figure 4a).

  3. Synthetic TTS Prosody Gap and Imperative Wait-100 Boundary: Comparing 2,025 curated vs. 3,195 expanded checkpoints (Table 9, Figure 4b) explains why Real-300 and Synthetic-300 diverge: adding 1,170 spontaneous Mandarin interview clips preserves or improves real human speech discrimination (0.9573 on Pikaia-Turn, 0.9460 on Pikaia-Turn-Mini, and 0.7198 [+6.96pp] on Pikaia-Turn-Nano), whereas CosyVoice-2 TTS lacks authentic pre-pause vowel lengthening and breath cues (0.9150 on Pikaia-Turn; 0.6137 on expanded Pikaia-Turn-Nano vs. 0.8216 on curated Pikaia-Turn-Nano). Finally, imperative wait phrases (Wait-100, e.g., Mandarin deng yixia, rang wo xiangxiang) carry terminal falling pitch and clean silence; with scarce imperative hold commands in natural research interviews and empty agent_text, 2.3B models misfire frequently (28.0%–42.0% hold accuracy), whereas Pikaia-Turn-Mini holds on 67.0% of cases.

Conclusion, Benchmark Availability, and Limitations

Summary of Findings

We introduced Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 to address a critical evaluation gap in modular bilingual (Mandarin Chinese and English) voice agents:

  1. Causal response-ready Evaluation Exposes Systematic Leaderboard Ranking Shifts: Task-dialogue leaderboards built on retrospective floor-end labels (LiveKit eot-bench) penalize natural mid-turn transition places by +38.47pp in low-FPR recall on identical Pikaia-Turn predictions, inverting top server rankings between zero-shot Turn-1 (#1 → #3) and Pikaia-Turn (#3 → #1, 394.4ms Wait@5%). Simultaneously, moving from short assistant queries to multi-clause interviews inverts audio-only rankings between Turn-1-Mini and Smart Turn v3.2 (#6 → #5, +19.41pp Tier 2 R@5%).

  2. response-ready Interview Supervision Transfers Upward on Public Leaderboards: Fine-tuning unmodified open-source Smart Turn v3.2 (8M) under our causal response-ready interview paradigm boosts Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 Tier 2 R@5% by +23.56pp (39.94%→62.59%, cutting full-benchmark Wait@5% by −104.4ms to 630.8ms) and vaults its standing on the public 13-system livekit.com/benchmarks/eot-bench leaderboard from #5 → #3 (≤2%) and #9 → #5#6 (≤10%) in English, and from #7 → #2#3 (≤5%) in Mandarin.

  3. Controlled Data and Architecture Gains Without Catastrophic Forgetting: Controlled Data × Architecture ablations across Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0, LiveKit eot-bench, and zero-context EasyTurn-800 demonstrate that training even unmodified open-source architectures on our curated corpus improves EasyTurn-800 (All-600 AUC 0.9435→0.9472 on Turn-1, 0.6626→0.7103 on Turn-1-Mini) with zero catastrophic forgetting, while modified Pikaia-Turn architectures eliminate domain-shift regression at expanded scale (Pikaia-Turn 394.4ms external LiveKit Wait@5%; Pikaia-Turn-Mini 395.3ms Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 Wait@5% and 97.0% EasyTurn backchannel hold; Pikaia-Turn-Nano −192.3ms CPU Wait@5% reduction) and retain full acoustic capacity on dyadic TurnBench Dev (91.70% Dev / 91.28% OOF recall under causal duplex VAD).

Benchmark Availability and Proprietary Model Scope

To support reproducible turn-taking evaluation across the research community while protecting participant privacy and anti-contamination integrity, Pikaia Interview EOU Benchmark v1.0.0 is publicly released with SHA256-verified manifests, standalone causal scoring tools (score.py), and dual-human blind audit records across two gated Hugging Face repositories under non-commercial Research Data Access Terms:

  • Tier 1 Development Split (N=100, Auto-Gated): https://huggingface.co/datasets/pikaia-ai/interview-eou-benchmark

  • Tier 2 Research Evaluation Split (N=1,100, Manual-Gated): https://huggingface.co/datasets/pikaia-ai/interview-eou-benchmark-research

Tier 3 (test_private, N=1,138) is retained strictly internally as a blind anti-overfitting holdout. The Pikaia-Turn model family weights (Pikaia-Turn, Pikaia-Turn-Mini, and Pikaia-Turn-Nano) and private interview training corpora are proprietary to Pikaia AI and are not open-sourced; all open-source baselines evaluated in this report (pipecat-ai/smart-turn-v3 [4], p99lab/turn-1, and p99lab/turn-1-mini [6]) are publicly available from their respective authors for independent reproduction on Tier 1 and Tier 2.

Limitations and Ethical Considerations

Several limitations bound our conclusions. First, primary benchmark evaluation is conducted at fixed causal pause cutoffs (300ms and paired 600ms) on recorded interviews rather than live closed-loop A/B deployments; offline recall at ≤5% FPR does not capture post-barge-in user repair dynamics. Second, while Tier 1 contains 12 speaker clusters (35 HOLDs) sufficient for coarse threshold anchoring, per-language calibration below 2% FPR benefits from larger calibration pools (150+ HOLDs per language) to bound binomial threshold variance. Third, as shown in Section 7, models adapted solely on natural interviews remain vulnerable in zero-context settings to explicit imperative “wait/hold on” utterances (Wait-100) unless paired with stronger context-dropout exposure and targeted wait-phrase negatives or lexical hold guardrails. Finally, all released interview recordings underwent consent verification, minor-age exclusion, and sensitive-content screening, and are distributed exclusively for non-commercial spoken-dialogue evaluation; voice biometric speaker identification, voice cloning, and commercial redistribution are strictly prohibited under the dataset access terms.
